title: Hebrews
tagline: An unsigned sermon, sent as a letter, that shows Jesus as the better priest, sacrifice and covenant, and urges weary believers to hold fast.

intro.text: Hebrews names neither its writer nor its readers. It calls itself a "word of exhortation", the phrase used for a synagogue sermon in Acts. It opens like an essay, preaches like a sermon, and ends like a letter, with news of Timothy and greetings from "they of Italy".

Its argument is that Jesus is better: better than the angels, than Moses, and than Aaron's priests, with a better covenant and a sacrifice offered once for all. Every stretch of teaching turns into an appeal: do not drift, draw near, hold fast.
The letter is woven from the Old Testament. Westcott counted 29 passages quoted directly, 23 of them from the Law and the Psalms, and 21 quoted nowhere else in the New Testament.

author.text: The letter never names its writer. He tells us only that he heard the gospel from people who had heard the Lord (2:3), that he knows Timothy (13:23), and that he hopes to see his readers again soon (13:19). He writes as one man (11:32). Who he was has been debated since the second century; Origen said that only God knows.

recipients.text: Believers who knew the old priestly system well and were tempted to drift away. In earlier days they had stood firm through public shame and the loss of their goods, but they had not yet suffered to the point of blood. Their first leaders had died. Where they lived is disputed: Jerusalem, Rome, Antioch, Ephesus and Alexandria have all been proposed. The title "To the Hebrews" was probably added by an early copyist.

writtenFrom.text: The letter does not say. Its one clue is "They of Italy salute you" (13:24). That can mean Italians living abroad sending greetings home, or people writing from Italy itself. Westcott warns that it can be read either way.

date.text: Written before about AD 96, when Clement of Rome made use of it. Whether it came before or after the Temple fell in AD 70 is disputed. Older scholars proposed dates from AD 61–62 (Bartlet) to AD 81–96 (Harnack and others).

occasion.text: The writer worries less about one named error than about drift and fatigue. His readers were in danger of letting the message slip, growing dull of hearing, skipping their meetings and throwing away their confidence. Pressure from outside added to the strain. Some sources read this as a pull back toward the old rites; others as a general loss of faith.

themes.text: God's final word. God once spoke in many ways through the prophets; now he has spoken by a Son, who is higher than the angels.
A better high priest. Jesus is a priest for ever "after the order of Melchisedec" (Ps 110:4). He was tested as we are, yet without sin, and he lives for ever to plead for his people.
A new and better covenant. Hebrews quotes the whole of Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant, then quotes it again, framing its central argument.
Once for all. The high priest went into the holiest place once every year, with the blood of animals. Christ entered once, with his own blood, and his one sacrifice does not need repeating.
Faith that endures. Faith is trust in what is hoped for and not yet seen. Chapter 11 tells the story of the faithful from Abel onward, and chapter 12 bids the reader run the race looking to Jesus.

Hold fast. Teaching alternates with warning and appeal; "let us" is repeated 13 times in 12 verses. Modern readers often count five warning passages. That is a reading aid, not the writer's own plan, though Westcott noted that solemn warnings fill the middle of each of the first three main parts.

keyVerses.why: The opening: the God who spoke through the prophets has now spoken by his Son.
The word of God is alive and cuts to the heart. It closes the warning drawn from Psalm 95.
A high priest who feels our weakness, and so an open invitation to come boldly for mercy.
Because he lives for ever, he is able to save completely those who come to God by him.
Christ entered the holy place once, with his own blood: the heart of the "once for all" theme.
The letter's description of faith, which opens the roll-call of the faithful.
The cloud of witnesses, and the call to run looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith.
"Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever."

views.label: Paul
views.holders: Pantaenus and Clement of Alexandria (late 2nd century); the Eastern churches; Athanasius (367); later the Latin West through Jerome and Augustine and the councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (419); in modern times Ebrard, Hofmann, Biesenthal, Kay and Easton's Bible Dictionary (1897).

argument.text: For: Timothy is mentioned (13:23), and Origen judged the thoughts to be the apostle's. Pantaenus explained the missing name: Paul, sent to the Gentiles, would not call himself apostle to the Hebrews. Clement added that Paul did not want to put off readers who distrusted him. The KJV's "me in my bonds" (10:34) seemed to point to Paul the prisoner, though Westcott's Greek text reads "the prisoners". Against: Paul says he received his gospel from no man, but this writer learned it from others (2:3), a point Westcott calls grave, even fatal. Origen found the Greek purer than Paul's, the writer always quotes the Greek Old Testament, and the church at Rome long disputed the claim.

views.label: Barnabas
views.holders: Tertullian (about AD 220); revived by Cameron in the 17th century; later Ritschl, Weiss, Renan, Salmon, Grau and Zahn (as listed by Dods and Westcott).

argument.text: For: it is the only named tradition besides Paul. Barnabas was a Levite, which would suit a writer so absorbed in priesthood. His nickname, "son of consolation", uses the same Greek word as the writer's "word of exhortation" (13:22). He was a Greek-speaking Cypriot in Paul's circle. Against: the tradition is found only in North Africa, and Origen does not know it. Dods and Rees treat the word match as coincidence. Davidson thinks his early story hardly fits 2:3.

views.label: Luke
views.holders: Clement of Alexandria (as translator of a letter Paul wrote in Hebrew); reported by Origen; Calvin (Luke or Clement); Delitzsch.

argument.text: For: ancient readers noticed that the style is like that of Acts, a likeness Westcott calls remarkable. Against: it may only mean the writer knew Luke's work or circle. If the letter was never translated from Hebrew, the main reason for naming Luke largely falls away. The Alexandrian cast of the letter's thought is not found in Luke.

views.label: Clement of Rome
views.holders: Reported by Origen; Eusebius (as the likelier translator); mentioned by Calvin.

argument.text: For: Clement's letter to Corinth (about AD 96) borrows heavily from Hebrews; its chapter 36 reworks Heb 1:3–4 and the psalms of 1:5–13. Jerome also noticed the likeness. Against: Westcott reads the parallels as Clement using Hebrews, just as he uses Paul's letters. Clement combines but does not create, and the depth of thought is far apart.

views.label: Apollos
views.holders: First suggested by Martin Luther (as reported by Westcott and Dods); then Bleek, Tholuck, Hilgenfeld, Lünemann, Reuss, Pfleiderer, Alford, Farrar, Plumptre and Kurtz; Bartlet in the 1911 Britannica, writing to Asia.

argument.text: For: Acts describes him as an Alexandrian Jew, "an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures", who showed from the scriptures that Jesus was the Christ. He belonged to Paul's circle. Davidson felt no better words could describe the writer of Hebrews. Against: no ancient writer suggests him. Westcott notes there is no evidence that Apollos wrote anything, and sees the guess as a reluctance to admit we do not know.

views.label: Priscilla (and Aquila)
views.holders: Adolf Harnack (1900, as reported by Dods and Rees); Bleek had almost argued for Aquila; Rendel Harris was sympathetic.

argument.text: For: the couple taught Apollos, worked with Paul, knew Timothy and hosted a church in their home at Rome. Harnack argued that the name was dropped because of prejudice against a woman teaching. Against: the writer speaks of himself as one man (11:32; 13:19, 22–23) and seems to be one of the leaders, as Dods points out. Rees answers that Paul also moves between "I" and "we".

views.label: Silas (Silvanus)
views.holders: Named as possible by Westcott; listed by Easton and in the ISBE.

argument.text: For: Silas belonged to Paul's circle, and 1 Peter was written "by Silvanus". Against: Westcott says only that the idea is consistent with what we know of him.

views.label: Others
views.holders: Mark (E. S. Lowndes, as reported by Westcott); Philip the deacon and Aristion (listed in the ISBE).

argument.text: Mostly guesswork. Rees calls these names little more than names to us. Jesus' own disciples are ruled out, because the writer heard the gospel second-hand (2:3).

views.label: Unknown
views.holders: Origen; Dods (1910), who thought it best to confess our ignorance; Rees in the ISBE (1915).

argument.text: Origen said that only God knows who wrote the letter. Dods preferred to admit ignorance, though he thought Aquila fitted a Roman destination as well as anyone. Rees leaned toward someone like Apollos but left the answer with God.

questions.question: Was Hebrews written before or after the Temple fell in AD 70?

views.label: Before AD 70
views.holders: Westcott (AD 64–67, most likely just before 67); Bartlet (AD 61–62); Smith's Bible Dictionary (AD 62–64); Salmon (AD 63); Ménégoz (AD 64–67); Riehm, Lünemann, Hilgenfeld, Weiss, Beyschlag, Schürer and Godet (about AD 66); Bleek (AD 68–69); Easton.

argument.text: The priests' service is described as still going on: there "are" priests who offer gifts (8:4), and the sacrifices would surely have "ceased to be offered" if they had worked (10:2). The old order is "ready to vanish away" (8:13), and the readers "see the day approaching" (10:25). A writer arguing that the old system was passing would surely have mentioned the Temple's fall if it had happened. Timothy is still alive and recently freed (13:23).

views.label: After AD 70
views.holders: Harnack, Pfleiderer, von Soden, Holtzmann and McGiffert (AD 81–96, as listed by Dods); Rees in the ISBE (about AD 80 or a little later).

argument.text: The writer always describes the tabernacle of Exodus, never Herod's Temple, and some of the objects he lists were never in the second Temple. Clement of Rome also speaks of ended rites in the present tense. A writer far from Jerusalem might leave its fall unmentioned. Timothy was young and could have lived on. The first leaders have died (13:7), the "former days" lie well in the past (10:32), and the readers have had time to grow dull (5:12). Both sides agree on an upper limit of about AD 96.

questions.question: Where did the first readers live?

views.label: Jerusalem or Palestine
views.holders: The tradition from Clement of Alexandria onward; Westcott (Jerusalem or its neighbourhood); Smith's Bible Dictionary; Easton.

argument.text: For: near the Temple the pull of the sacrifices would be strongest, and the Jerusalem church was wholly Hebrew until Hadrian's reign. Against: the letter is in polished Greek. Jerusalem's first believers did not hear the gospel second-hand (2:3), would hardly be scolded for producing no teachers (5:12), and received gifts rather than gave them (6:10). The Temple is never named.

views.label: Rome or Italy
views.holders: First suggested by Wetstein; Alford, Holtzmann and Zahn (as listed by Dods); Harnack; discussed by Davidson.

argument.text: For: "They of Italy salute you" most naturally reads as Italians abroad sending greetings home. Clement of Rome is the first to use the letter, and Rome had many Jewish Christians. Zahn suggested one of the house churches greeted in Romans 16. Against: a Roman church would expect some word about Nero's persecution, and "ye have not yet resisted unto blood" fits Rome badly after AD 64. Westcott warns that 13:24 can be read either way.

views.label: A Jewish community in the East, outside Jerusalem
views.holders: Davidson.

argument.text: For: it fits a Greek-speaking Jewish church with a Greek outlook. Against: it cannot be pinned to a place.

views.label: Antioch or another Syrian city
views.holders: Rendall (as quoted by Dods).

argument.text: For: Antioch had large Greek-speaking Jewish-Christian churches. Against: Dods asks how the church that launched Paul's mission could deserve the rebuke for immaturity in 5:11–14.

views.label: Ephesus or Asia
views.holders: Bartlet, in the 1911 Britannica.

argument.text: For: Timothy was based at Ephesus, and Apollos was connected with it. Against: it remains a guess.

views.label: Alexandria
views.holders: Mentioned as an option in the ISBE and by Davidson.

argument.text: For: the letter's thought has an Alexandrian cast. Against: Alexandria itself held that the letter was written to Palestine.

views.label: Gentile Christians
views.holders: Von Soden, Schürer, Weizsäcker, Jülicher and McGiffert (as listed by Dods).

argument.text: For: the "first principles" of 6:1–2 sound like teaching for converts from paganism, and "departing from the living God" (3:12) sounds like a lapse into it. Against: the whole argument assumes readers who revere Moses and Aaron. Westcott calls the theory an ingenious paradox.

views.label: No single church: a general sermon
views.holders: Reuss and Lipsius (as listed by Dods).

argument.text: For: there is no opening address. Against: personal details point to a definite group: their slowness to learn, their past sufferings, and their present trials.

questions.question: Is Hebrews a sermon or a letter?

views.label: A sermon: a "word of exhortation"
views.holders: Davidson (1882).

argument.text: Hebrews calls itself a "word of exhortation" (13:22), the same phrase used of a synagogue sermon in Acts 13:15. It speaks like a preacher: "whereof we speak", "we have many things to say", "the time would fail me to tell". Davidson sees it not as a treatise but as an appeal to hold fast, with the teaching serving that appeal.

views.label: Essay, sermon and letter in one
views.holders: Thomas Rees, in the ISBE (1915).

argument.text: Rees put it this way: Hebrews begins like an essay, goes on like a sermon, and ends like a letter. It opens with no greeting (1:1–4), but it closes with a request for prayer, a blessing, news of Timothy, greetings and a final grace. Rees treats the whole as one work.

views.label: A literary oration, perhaps once with an opening
views.holders: Deissmann and Overbeck (as reported in the ISBE).

argument.text: Deissmann called it a literary oration and allowed that it may once have had an opening address. Overbeck argued that an opening naming someone other than Paul was removed and the closing verses 13:22–25 added.

views.label: A sermon with chapter 13 added later
views.holders: Reuss (as reported by Dods); Wrede (as reported in the ISBE).

argument.text: On this view the letter-like ending was attached afterwards, perhaps for a particular group. Dods and Rees both reject it.

questions.question: What danger was the writer facing?

views.label: A pull back toward Judaism and its rites
views.holders: Davidson; Dods; Easton.

argument.text: Dods describes a gradual, almost unconscious doubt that dulled hope and slackened energy. The argument that Christ's priesthood replaces the old one would speak to readers drawn back to the old rites.

views.label: A general loss of faith
views.holders: Von Soden (as reported in the ISBE).

argument.text: The danger is weariness and unbelief rather than a return to Judaism. Rees answers that the Jewish framing of the whole argument still implies Jewish readers.

views.label: Shock at the fall of the Temple
views.holders: Discussed by Davidson, who doubts it.

argument.text: Some have suggested that the Temple's destruction shook the readers. Davidson weighs the idea and doubts it.

claim.text: Clement uses Hebrews without naming it. His chapter 36 reworks Heb 1:3–4 and the chain of psalms in 1:5–13.
Marcion's list of Paul's letters leaves Hebrews out.
The list does not mention Hebrews. It counts letters of Paul to only seven churches.
Eusebius says Irenaeus mentioned Hebrews in a book of discourses. A later report says he denied that Paul wrote it.
Both treat Hebrews as Paul's letter. Clement adds that Paul wrote it in Hebrew and Luke translated it.
Gaius counts only thirteen letters of Paul. Eusebius remarks that some at Rome still did not count Hebrews as the apostle's.
According to a later report by Photius, Hippolytus denied that Paul wrote it.
Tertullian knows it as a letter of Barnabas. He quotes 6:4–8 as carrying weight, but less than an apostle's, since it comes from a companion of the apostles.
Origen finds the Greek purer than Paul's but the thoughts the apostle's. Some, he says, name Clement or Luke; who actually wrote it, only God knows.
Eusebius counts fourteen letters of Paul as well known, but notes that some reject Hebrews because the church of Rome disputes it. (His list of disputed books in 3.25 does not include Hebrews.)
Athanasius lists fourteen letters of Paul, placing Hebrews after 2 Thessalonians and before 1 Timothy.
Jerome reports that many did not count Hebrews as Paul's because its style and language differ. Others credited it to Barnabas, Luke or Clement.
The list reads: "Of the Apostle Paul, thirteen Epistles, of the same to the Hebrews, one." Hebrews is accepted, but still counted apart.
Augustine sometimes cites Hebrews as Paul's and sometimes without a name, deferring to the churches of the East.
Now the list reads: "Epistles of Paul in number fourteen."

canon.label: Reformation era (16th century)
canon.who: Cajetan, Erasmus, Luther, Calvin and Beza

claim.text: Doubts about who wrote it return. Luther suggests Apollos. Calvin sees no reason to think Paul wrote it, yet receives the letter as apostolic and suggests Luke or Clement.

parallels.title: The Day of Atonement and Hebrews 9

pairs.note: Not at all times within the veil; the high priest goes in once every year (also 9:25; 10:3).
"Once a year" in Leviticus; "once" for all with Christ (also 7:27; 10:10).
No one else in the tabernacle; "the high priest alone".
A bullock for himself first, then the people's goat (Lev 16:11, 15); "for himself, and for the errors of the people" (also 7:27; 5:3).
Blood sprinkled on and before the mercy seat; "not without blood" (9:7); "by his own blood he entered in once".
The blood of bulls and goats (Lev 16:5, 11, 15); "the blood of goats and calves" (9:12) and "of bulls and of goats" (also 10:4).
A cloud of incense covers the mercy seat; the golden censer.
The scapegoat bears the people's sins. Hebrews does not cite it directly; "to bear the sins of many" echoes Isa 53:12.

claim.text: Hebrews 9 reads Christ's work through the Day of Atonement. The yearly entry of the high priest, alone and with animal blood, is set against Christ's single entry with his own blood. The carcasses burned "without the camp" in Lev 16:27 return in Heb 13:11–13, where Jesus suffers outside the gate.

pairs.note: Abraham returns from the slaughter of the kings.
King of Salem and priest of the most high God; Hebrews reads his names as "King of righteousness" and "King of peace".
Genesis says nothing of his parents, birth or death; Hebrews reads that silence: "without father, without mother… abideth a priest continually".
He blessed Abram; "the less is blessed of the better".
Abram gave him tithes; so Levi, still in Abraham's loins, paid tithes too.

claim.text: Hebrews draws on two passages: the meeting in Genesis 14 and the oath of Psalm 110:4, "Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek", quoted at 5:6, 7:17 and 7:21. Westcott notes that the writer reads the record of Scripture, including its silences, rather than the historical man. He passes over the bread and wine, presenting Melchizedek as a priest who blesses rather than one who sacrifices.

timelines.title: The hall of faith, in story order

events.label: Abel offers a more excellent sacrifice
Abraham leaves home, not knowing where
Isaac and Jacob live in tents
Joseph speaks of the Exodus and his bones
Moses chooses God's people and keeps the Passover

claim.text: Hebrews 11 walks through the Old Testament from Abel to the prophets. Here each example is placed in the order of the Old Testament story, not by date. Hebrews names the judges in its own order (Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, then David before Samuel). Westcott thought they were listed by popular fame, and that David and Samuel are paired as the great king and the great prophet.

stops.name: Rome
stops.note: Wetstein, Alford, Holtzmann, Zahn and Harnack. Dods reads "they of Italy" (13:24) as Italians abroad sending greetings home.

stops.name: Alexandria
stops.note: Mentioned as an option in the ISBE and by Davidson.

claim.text: Five places proposed for the letter's first readers. None is named in the letter; each pin shows a view and who held it, not a conclusion. Others thought of a Jewish community elsewhere in the East, of Gentile Christians, or of no single church at all.

Each line joins an Old Testament book to the chapter of Hebrews that quotes it, counting formal quotations, verbal uses and repeats (close echoes are left out). Westcott counted 29 distinct passages, 23 of them from the Law and the Psalms, and found that the writer follows the Greek Old Testament throughout, except at 10:30. Psalm 95 and Psalm 110 are quoted most often.

steps.label: The prophets
steps.note: God spoke in many ways through the prophets; in these last days he has spoken by his Son.

steps.label: Angels
steps.note: "So much better than the angels." The first "better" of the letter.

steps.label: Moses
steps.better: more glory: the builder, not the house
steps.note: Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house; Christ as a Son over it.

steps.label: Joshua
steps.better: the rest Joshua did not give
steps.note: The KJV reads "Jesus" in 4:8, the Greek form of the name Joshua.

steps.label: Aaron and the Levitical priests
steps.better: a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek
steps.note: Many priests died in turn; he continues for ever. "The less is blessed of the better."

steps.label: The first covenant
steps.better: a better covenant, on better promises

steps.label: The earthly sanctuary
steps.better: the true tabernacle, in heaven itself
steps.note: "A greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands."

steps.label: Animal sacrifices
steps.better: better sacrifices: his own blood, once for all
steps.note: "How much more shall the blood of Christ…"

steps.label: Earthly goods, country and life
steps.better: a better possession, country and resurrection
steps.note: A better and lasting substance, a heavenly country, a better resurrection, "some better thing for us".

steps.label: Abel's blood
steps.better: the blood that speaks better things
steps.note: Abel's blood cried out from the ground (Gen 4:10); Jesus' blood speaks better things.

claim.text: The Greek word for "better" (kreittōn) appears 13 times in 12 verses, and other comparisons ("more excellent", "more glory", "how much more") carry the same idea. The ladder follows the order of the argument, from the prophets to the blood of Jesus. Davidson and Dods describe the same sequence.
